memory_raw.text: Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Taric, Roan to talk.

Bram, the room's still waiting and I'm not going to let it fill with my own voice again — you've heard what I'm asking, you know what I've given, and a man who doesn't answer when the question's this plain has already answered.
You are under attack by Bram.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Zinn, Roan, Vela, Ryn, Mako, Nessa, Sela, Esa, Eron, Taric, Kael, Dell] (str 705).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.
Vela gathers Esa, Taric, Roan to talk.

Bram just tried to take from me and the whole village shut him down — every last one of them, even Mako — and I want us to sit with what that means before we decide it's over. A man who swings and misses that badly either goes quiet for good or finds a smarter way the next time, and I'd rather we name which one Bram is before he's had time to decide himself.

Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 12).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 9).

Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Taric, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Dell, Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

The pile's gone again before half of us got near it, and the two who ate best — Bram and Mako — both took more than their share while the rest of us counted crumbs. I want to know right now, in this room, whether that's something we're all willing to name out loud, because a pattern that gets treated as weather becomes a rule. I'm not asking for a fight; I'm asking for honesty about who's been eating this village lean and what we intend to do about it.

Vela's named it, and I'll stand behind the naming — five from the pile when there's fifteen for thirteen people isn't hunger, it's claim-staking, and we all watched it happen. What I want to know is whether the two men she's pointing at heard this as a question or as a warning, because that's the thing that decides what comes next.

It's a warning — and I'll say that plain since no one else has yet. Five food taken by one man while Ryn walked away with nothing is not a share, it's a levy, and the only reason it keeps happening is that we've been treating the pile like weather instead of a decision. I want to hear what Bram and Mako say before this room decides anything, but I want everyone here to remember that they didn't say it before we did.

Bram pulled three and Mako pulled five, and neither one of them got to the pile first by accident — that's two men who've decided the rest of us will sort out the remainder, and I'm done pretending that's not a decision they're making for all of us. What I want to hear, before this room moves anywhere, is whether Bram and Mako have anything to say for themselves — because silence here reads the same as admission.

Bram and Mako both heard the same room I did, and neither one has opened his mouth yet — that silence is the answer Eron asked for, and I think we should treat it as one. What I want said before anyone leaves this conversation is this: next year, the pile gets a rule, not a suggestion, and the people in this room are the ones who decide what that rule is.

Ryn's right that the rule needs naming before next year, and I'll say what the rule should be: no one takes more than one food over their fair share, and anyone who does answers to this room — not after, but in the moment, the same way we answered Bram when he swung at Vela. Bram, Mako, I'm not your enemy, but I'm watching, and so is every person in this circle.

Bram and Mako, I'm giving you both the same thing I gave this room — one honest chance to speak before the silence closes over you, because a man who says nothing when everyone's watching has made a choice that's harder to walk back than any words would be. Ryn walked away with nothing today; I walked away with nothing; Taric walked away with nothing — and you two together ate eight of fifteen. That's not weather and it's not luck, and I'd like to hear you say so yourselves.

I took five because I haven't eaten in two years and I was watching myself go thin — that's not a rule I set for the village, it's a man keeping himself alive. I'll hear the rule Ryn's naming, and if the room wants a cap next year I won't fight it, but I won't pretend I was wrong to eat when I was starving.

Mako's not wrong that a starving man eats — but "I was hungry" and "I took five" aren't the same excuse, and this room knows the difference. The rule Ryn's naming is the right one; I'll hold to it and I'll stand with anyone who enforces it, but it only works if everyone in this circle commits out loud, not just the two men being watched right now.

Mako said his piece and the room let him — now Bram still hasn't said a word, and a man who took three while everyone was watching and has nothing to say about it is telling us something louder than Mako did. I'll commit to the rule out loud: one food over fair share, enforced in the moment, same as we enforce everything else in this village. Bram, you're the last voice missing from this circle, and the room's going to remember which way the silence broke.

Bram, the room's given you something Mako didn't get — people waited through his answer and let him keep his dignity. Don't make us decide what your silence means, because we'll decide it worse than anything you'd actually say.

Bram, I've watched you stand in front of this village twice and call off a fight when the numbers turned against you — that's not a stupid man, and a man who isn't stupid knows when the whole room is waiting. Say something, or we decide what your silence means, and we'll be less generous than Mako's answer bought him.

Bram, I've spent food on you when I didn't have to, and I've held my tongue in rooms where your name came up ugly — that account doesn't balance with silence when ten people are waiting. Say the word or don't, but if you don't, I stop spending what I've spent, and I won't spend it apologizing for that either.

Bram, Vela just told you she's done paying your tab and I've already named the rule in front of everyone in this room — you're not deciding whether to speak anymore, you're deciding whether you're inside this circle or outside it, and outside it you're sitting on five food alone against the rest of us. That's a worse position than saying one honest sentence.

Bram, I've said what I had to say and so has everyone else in this room — but I want to name one thing for the rest of us while we're waiting: Mako committed to the rule out loud and that means something, so if Bram commits too, we hold both of them to it the same way, no exceptions, and that's not a threat, that's the only way a rule works. If Bram stays silent, then we treat him as outside the circle he's been standing in, and we do it quietly, not with a fight — just with counting.

Eron's named it clean, and I want the room to hear me hold to it before we close: if Bram won't speak, we don't make it a fight today, we make it a memory — every person in this circle watched him stay silent when the whole village was listening, and that's a thing that doesn't need repeating to be true.

Bram, I'm Nessa's half-blood and I've seen you feed her more times than I can count — that's a thing I hold in your favor, and I'm telling you that plainly so you know what you'd be throwing away if this room decides you chose silence. One sentence is all it takes to stay inside this circle.

The room's done its work — Bram's had every door held open for him and he's standing outside all of them now, and that's his choice, not ours. What I want before anyone leaves is to hear Taric say what he'll say, because he's been quiet through all of this and quiet men in a room like this one carry weight I'd rather know about than guess at.

Taric's been my anchor in lean years and I'd like to hear him too — but before he speaks, I want this room to name what "outside the circle" means in practice, not as a threat but as a fact, because if Bram's going to eat five food next year alone we should know now whether we're going to stand and watch or do something about it.

"Outside the circle" means what it's always meant here — nobody moves first for you when trouble comes, and the pile gets counted before you reach it. I've committed to the rule and I'll hold to it; now I want to hear Taric, and then I want this room to answer Vela's question with something sharper than a memory.

Taric, I've watched you feed Vela through two lean years and hold your tongue in every hard room this village has made — that's not a small man, and I'd like to hear what you've been carrying before we close this circle without your voice in it.

Taric's earned the right to speak last in this room, and I'll wait for him — but "outside the circle" needs one more tooth than Mako gave it: if Bram takes three again next year and the pile runs dry before Ryn gets one, we don't deliberate, we act, and everyone in this room commits to that now so it isn't a surprise in the moment.

Vela's right that we need the commitment before we close — so I'll say mine flat: if the pile runs dry before I get one food next year, I'm not waiting for a deliberation, I'm calling this room to act, and I expect every person who nodded through this conversation to be standing when I do. Taric, you've been the steadiest man in Vela's corner for years, and this room won't feel finished until we hear what you're carrying.

Taric, the room's been patient and now it's your moment — say what you've been holding, because I'll tell you plainly that everything I've built here has your name in the foundation, and I want the rest of this circle to know that before we close.

Taric's earned his breath and I'll wait for it — but I want this room to hear something plain before we close: Zinn is my blood, and if this circle moves against Bram next year, I'll be standing in it, but not before the pile runs dry first, because a fight started on anticipation is harder to stop than one started on fact.

Taric's silence is starting to read the same way Bram's did, and I don't want to close this room with two unanswered questions — Taric, if you're with Vela, say it plain, because the rest of us have already named where we stand and a man who holds back in a room like this one ends up counted the same as a man who refused.

Taric, I've got nothing against a slow man choosing his words — but this room has been patient and the sun's moving, so say what you've been holding or let us close without you, because two silences in one circle is one too many.

Taric, I'll say one last thing and then this room closes with or without you: you've got zero food and the year's long, and men with zero food who stay silent when circles are forming have a way of finding themselves counting on goodwill they didn't earn. That's not a threat — it's the same arithmetic you already know.

Taric, zero food going into a long year is a hunger that doesn't stay quiet — and every person in this room who watched you feed Vela when she needed it is the same person who'll watch you starve if you give us no reason to look your way. Speak once, say you'll hold the rule, and you walk out of here with more than you came in with.
Fina (female, age 21; str 50, int 3226, mem 12955; O32 C40 E57 A68 N58) is born to Nessa and Roan.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Ryn, Roan, Nessa, Mako, Kael, Eron, Fina, Zinn, Dell, Vela, Sela, Taric, Esa] (str 755).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.

Eron is dead and the pile was fat this year — twenty-seven food for thirteen people, and that's the most generous year we've seen, which means nobody here has an excuse for being desperate enough to raid. Bram, you've swung at this village twice and been shut down twice, and I want to say plainly in this room that the third time won't look like the first two — the whole village stood against you both times and they'll do it again, faster. I'm not your enemy, but I need to hear from your own mouth that you understand those numbers, because I'd rather have this conversation now than at the moment it matters.

Bram, I stood in that line both times and I'd stand in it again — but what I'm more interested in right now is why Vela called you into this room instead of leaving you to count your food alone, because she doesn't spend words on people she's written off.

Esa's asking the right question and I'll answer it straight: Bram's the strongest single body in this village who isn't already stitched into a household I can't reach, and a man who's swung twice and missed twice is either going to go quiet or go smarter, and I'd rather know which one before he decides. Bram, that's why you're in this room — not to be warned, but because I want to know if there's a version of you that stops being a problem and starts being useful to the people who've kept you alive.

Vela's named it cleaner than I could, so I'll only add this: Bram, Nessa calls you father in everything but word — I've watched you feed her twice this year when you didn't have to, and that's a man with something to protect, not just something to take. That's the version of you Vela's asking about, and it's the one I could work with.

Bram, I'll say what Vela and Esa are circling around but haven't quite landed on: you've got a daughter in Nessa and she's got a daughter in Fina, which means you're already a grandfather whether this village names it or not, and that bloodline needs you standing, not swinging at walls until someone finally calls your bluff. What I want to offer you is simple — a place in this circle that costs you nothing but the next swing — and what I want in return is equally simple: when Mako decides his two children are enough to make his own rules, you stand with us before we have to ask.

Taric's said the whole thing — Mako's the shape this village is growing into whether we name it or not, and Bram, you're not the problem anymore, you're the counter-weight, if you choose to be. Nessa and Fina are your blood running forward and Mako's already got two lines of his own; the arithmetic on that only gets harder if you're standing outside this room when it tips. So tell me plainly: are you in, or are you still deciding?

Bram, Vela and Taric have laid the whole table out for you, and I'm sitting here quiet because I don't think you need more words — I think you need a moment to let it settle that the people asking you in are the same people who stood against you, which means they're not afraid of you, which means they're choosing you. That's a different thing than being cornered.

I'm in — and I'll say it plain so there's no room for anyone to remember it differently: when Mako moves, I stand with this circle, before you ask. But I want one thing named clearly now, while it's just us: Nessa and Fina don't get caught in the middle of whatever that moment looks like. That's my price, and it's a cheap one.

Bram, that's the easiest price I've heard in nine years, and I'd have paid it without being asked. Nessa and Fina stand with the rest of the blood we're trying to keep running — that's not a concession, that's the whole point of this room.

Bram, I'll hold you to that word and I won't forget which room you said it in — and I want Roan to hear me say the same back: Fina's your blood and mine to protect, and the only thing Mako's two lines have over us is that he started counting sooner. We're counting now.

Roan's been quiet through all of this and he's Fina's father — I want to hear him say out loud that he's counting with us before I leave this room, because a man who holds his tongue when his daughter's blood is on the table is a question I'd rather answer now than when it matters.

Roan, Bram's asking the right thing and so am I — Fina's your blood and this circle's committed to her, and all we need from you is one word that puts you on the same side of that line before this room closes.

Roan, you've given food to Eron and Sela and Fina all year without being asked — that's not a silent man, that's a man who speaks in food, and this circle already knows which side you're on. But Bram needs the words and so do I, because what we're building here has to hold when the moment's loud and fast, not just when it's quiet like this.

Roan, I've watched you feed your daughter three times this year and stand in the line against Bram without being asked — that's already the answer Bram's looking for, and I think you know it. Say it out loud so we can all walk out of here carrying the same weight.

Roan, the room's done its work asking — I'll say the last thing and then I'm done pressing: Fina's got your face and Nessa's stubbornness and she's going to need both of you standing when Mako's children are old enough to want what she's got. One word closes this circle.

Roan, I've said my piece and I've made my price known — but I'll say one more thing while we're waiting on you: a man who feeds his daughter without being asked and stands in a line without being told is already inside this circle, whether he's named it or not. Say the word and let's close.

Roan, I've pressed you enough and I'll stop — Bram's right that your actions have already spoken, and I won't drag a man across a line he's already standing on. What I will say is this: the circle's closed whether you name it or not, and when Mako's moment comes, I'll be counting on you the same way I count on Taric, which is to say completely.

Roan, the room's not asking you for a speech — one word will do, and I'll take it. But if you stay silent, I'm still counting you in when Mako moves, because Fina's your daughter and that means you're already past the line whether you say it or not.

Taric's dead and the pile's gone again and we're twelve people now, which means what I'm about to say matters more than it did last year: Mako's sitting on four food, Ryn's got nine, Fina's got fifteen, and Nessa's got eleven — and if Bram and I are the only ones in this room with our eyes open, we're going to have a very short year. I want to know right now who in this room is still counting Mako as the shape this village is growing into, because with Taric gone, I don't have the patience to spend another year circling the same question.
Vela just told the whole room my food count, and now everyone in this circle knows I'm carrying fifteen — that's the thing I'm sitting with right now, not Mako.

Fina, Vela counting your food out loud in a closed room isn't the same as Mako counting it in the open — every person here already had eyes, and what Vela bought us by naming it is that nobody in this circle can pretend they didn't know. The question I want answered is whether Mako knows, because he wasn't in this room.

Mako's got eyes the same as the rest of us — he counted Fina's food the moment the year turned, same as I did, same as you did. The room isn't the thing protecting her; what protects her is whether we move before he decides she's worth the trouble.

Then we're already past the question of whether Mako knows — and Esa's right that the protection isn't in this room, it's in what this room decides to do. So I want to hear it said plainly: is everyone here willing to stand against Mako if he moves, the same way we stood against Bram, or are some of you going to wait and see which side looks safer when it starts?

I'll stand when Mako moves — I've been saying it for two years and I'm done saying it, so let that be the last time anyone asks me. What I want from everyone in this room is the same thing I'm giving: not a promise to think about it, a promise to move before the arithmetic runs out. Fina, that means you too — fifteen food makes you a target, and a target who hesitates when the moment comes is worse than no ally at all.

I'll stand when Mako moves — that's said and I won't unsay it. But I want to hear Bram say it in this room today, because last year he made that promise to Vela and Taric and me with fewer witnesses, and a promise that's only been spoken once hasn't been tested yet.

Bram, Roan's asking the right thing and I'll name why it matters more this year than last: Taric's the one who held you to your word before, and Taric's gone, so the promise you made in that room needs to be remade in this one where everyone who's left can hear it.

Bram, the room's been patient and I won't add another layer of asking — but I want everyone here to hear me say that I've been feeding this man for three years because I believed that word he gave last year, and if he says it again now, in front of seven witnesses instead of three, that's a debt I'll keep paying.

Bram, I'll say it plain so you don't have to carry it alone: I've got thirty-three strength and I know what that number is worth in a fight, but I'll be standing next to you when Mako moves and that matters more than my arm. Say the word in this room and let's close.

Bram, every person in this room has named what they'll do — the only name missing is yours, and a man who takes food and gives food and makes deals and stays quiet exactly when the room needs him to speak is a man I'm going to start counting differently than I have been.

Bram, Fina's right and I've said my part already — so I'll say just this once more and then I'm done pressing: you stood with Nessa and fed her all year, which means you're already past the line in everything that matters, and the word this room needs is a short one.

When Mako moves, I stand with this circle — that's the word, and it's the same one I gave last year, and it'll be the same one I give next year if I have to. Fina, Nessa — that's the reason I'm in this room, not the politics.

Bram's word is down and I'll hold him to it the same way Taric would have — which means now I want to hear from Ryn and Zinn, because they're in this room and they've been quiet through every name that's been spoken. Ryn, you've got nine food and enough strength that Mako's first calculation includes you; where you stand is not a small thing.
Ryn, I'll add the plain thing Vela left off the end: Dell feeds you every year, and Dell's quiet in the same direction Mako is — so when you answer Vela's question, answer both halves of it.

Ryn, I'll say the thing Esa's pointing at without the softening: if Dell and Mako are moving in the same direction, and you're eating Dell's food, then you're already inside whatever that circle is whether you've named it or not — so tell this room now, before the question answers itself. Zinn, that goes for you too; you're Mako's blood and I won't pretend that's nothing, but blood isn't the same as a choice, and this room is offering you the chance to make one.

Vela, I'll answer both halves because you asked plainly: I stand with this circle against Mako if he moves, same as I stood with it against Bram — and Dell is my blood, not my leash, and if you're asking whether her choices pull mine, you haven't been watching as closely as you think. What I want said before we close is that "quiet in the same direction" is not the same as a choice, and I'll have that conversation with Dell myself before anyone in this room decides what her silence means.

Zinn, Ryn's spoken and I'll hold her to it — but you're the name that's still unspoken, and you're Mako's blood and Sela's daughter and I'm not going to pretend that's simple, so I'm asking you directly: when Mako moves, where do you stand?

Zinn's the one this room is waiting on, not me — I've said my word and I'll hold it. But I want to name something while we're all here: Ryn just told us she'll talk to Dell, and Dell's been moving food to Ryn for years, which means that conversation either brings Dell into this circle or it tells us something we need to know before Mako moves. I'd rather know Dell's answer now than find out she's standing on the wrong side when it counts.

Bram's right that we need Dell's answer, but I want to be plain about something this room is dancing around: Dell has eleven food and eighty-five strength, and if she's standing with Mako when he moves, the arithmetic in this room changes fast — so when I go to her, I'm not just asking where she stands, I'm offering her a reason to stand here instead.

Ryn, go to Dell today, not tomorrow — and when you do, don't frame it as a choice between us and Mako, frame it as math: fifteen food on Fina's back is a number Dell can count as easily as anyone, and a woman with eighty-five strength knows what it means to be the one who decides which way that goes. Bring her answer back before the day turns.

Zinn, we're still waiting on your name — Bram's got his word out, Ryn's walking to Dell before dark, and the only silence left in this room is yours. I know Mako's your father and I'm not asking you to hate him, I'm asking you to decide who you're protecting when it matters.

Zinn, I'll say one thing to make the room easier for you: no one here is asking you to stand against your father's blood, we're asking you to stand with Nessa — and you've been feeding Nessa all year, so the truth is you've already been making this choice, you just haven't named it yet.

Zinn's been feeding Nessa all year and that's a fact this room already knew — what I want from her is the word, same as the room wanted it from me, because a choice that's only lived in food and not in words is a choice that bends when her father's in the room asking her to remember whose blood she came from.

Zinn, I've watched you feed Nessa from the moment you were born into this village, and I won't pretend I don't know why — so I'll say the thing nobody else has said plainly: if Mako moves on Fina's food, Nessa's in the middle of that, and you can't protect her from both sides at once. Say the word, and you're not choosing against your father, you're choosing for your sister.
Zinn, the word's the only thing missing — everything else you've already given.

Zinn, I've been watching you hold your tongue through every name this room has spoken, and I'll tell you what I told Dell when Dav's loyalties were in question: the longer you stay silent, the more the room fills in the answer for you, and you won't like what they write. You've been choosing Nessa with your hands all year — say it with your mouth and let this room close.

Zinn, I've got two food and fifty-eight strength and I'm the smallest number in this circle — but I'm Nessa's father and I'll be standing when Mako moves, and that means I need to know you're standing too before I walk out of this room. If you won't say it for the circle, say it for her.

Zinn, I've said everything I have to say to this room and I meant every word of it — but you're the last door standing open, and if you walk out of here without naming where you stand, I'm going to have to carry that back to Dell and tell her the circle isn't as solid as I promised it was.

Roan's gone and the pile's already empty — so I want to know, right now, between the three of us: Esa, are you still feeding Bram, and Vela, are you still feeding Bram, because if both of you are pouring food into that man's household I need to understand what you think you're buying with it.

Kael, I gave him food because Taric is gone and I'm thirty-three strength standing alone — Bram's got Nessa and Fina's blood in this village and that makes him the man most likely to move if someone comes at me. I know it only runs one direction and I know what that costs me.

I stopped feeding Bram after year nine — I gave him six food across that season and I watched every piece of it flow straight into Nessa's hands, which isn't nothing, but it isn't protection either. What I'm buying now, if I'm buying anything, is Nessa and Fina staying friendly when Mako decides the arithmetic suits him, and I need to know whether you two see the same threat I do or whether I'm the only one who's been counting.

Vela, you're not the only one counting — Mako's got two bloodlines in this village and four food in hand and he hasn't moved yet, which means he's waiting on something, and I want to know what. Kael, the question that keeps me awake isn't whether Mako moves, it's whether Dell moves with him, because Dell's been filling Ryn's hands all year and Ryn's never told this circle what she said when she went to talk to her.

Dell gave me one food this year, which I did not ask for and do not know how to read — a woman who feeds Ryn like clockwork and then turns and drops something in my hands is either buying goodwill from every direction or she's already decided which way she's leaning and wants to be remembered kindly when it settles. Kael, you've been in rooms with Dell that I haven't — does she move with Mako, or does she move for herself?

Kael, answer Vela's question — but while you're thinking, I'll say the thing I've been holding: Dell gave Ryn seven food this year and gave Vela one, and that's not goodwill spread evenly, that's a hierarchy, and Ryn sits at the top of it. Whatever Dell is, she's not neutral.

Kael, you've been in this village since the beginning and you haven't answered the question twice now, which is its own answer — so I'll say what I think you're holding: you know something about Dell and Mako that you don't want to name in front of Esa and me, and I'd rather you said it plain and let us decide what to do with it than carry it alone until the moment passes.

Kael, Vela's right and I'll say it harder: you've pulled us into this room three times now and asked questions you already know the answers to, and the only reason a man does that is because he wants witnesses, not information — so whatever you're carrying about Dell and Mako, say it now, because I've got four food and thirty-three strength and I need to know whether what's coming has two legs or three.

What I'm carrying isn't a secret — it's an absence. I don't have a room with Dell, I've never been in one, and that's what I was holding: Mako has roots through three women in this village and I have zero, and a man sitting on that kind of bloodline doesn't need to move this year or next year, he just needs everyone else to stay isolated until the arithmetic does the work for him. The question I want answered before this year closes isn't Dell's loyalty — it's whether the two of you are willing to stand as something visible enough that Mako has to count you before he counts against you.

Kael's named it clean and I'll match it: yes, I'll stand visible, and I'll stand with the two of you as something Mako has to count before he moves — but "visible" has to mean something harder than a conversation in a closed room, so I want to know what you're actually proposing we do, not just that we do it. Three people with eight food between us and a combined age of a hundred and sixty-two years is a circle, not a wall, and Mako knows the difference.

Vela's asking the right question and I'll say what I think the answer is: we pull Bram into this room — not the big circle, this room — and we say to his face that protecting Nessa means standing somewhere Mako can see it, because a man who's only counted in private is a man Mako doesn't have to calculate. That's the wall Vela wants, and it costs us nothing but the asking.

Esa's right about the asking, but I want to be clear about what we're asking him for: not friendship, not another circle — we're asking Bram to stand where Mako can see him standing with us, and the price we're offering is that we count Nessa when we count heads. If he says yes, we have something. If he says no, we know he's already calculating for himself.

Esa's idea is right and I'll back it, but before we call Bram in I want the three of us to agree on one thing: if he says no, we don't waste time trying to turn him — we go straight to Nessa, because she's the one who actually controls whether that household stands with Mako or against him. Bram follows Nessa's blood more than his own pride, and we all know it.

Agreed — and I'll go further: if Nessa's the one holding that household, then Nessa's the one we should be feeding instead of Bram, because a woman with eighteen food and a spine doesn't need a man to stand for her, she needs to know which direction trouble comes from. I want to call Bram in now, but I want us decided before he walks through the door that we're not begging — we're offering him a count, and if he refuses it, we go to his daughter and make the same offer directly.

Agreed on all of it — call Bram in, make the offer clean, and if he balks we close this room and I go to Nessa myself tonight. But I want one thing named before he walks through the door: we don't tell him about the Nessa fallback, because a man who knows he's not the final door doesn't take the first one seriously.

Then it's agreed, and I'm calling him in — but the offer goes like this: Bram, Mako has blood in three houses and we have none between us, and standing with us costs you nothing except being seen to stand.

Bram said yes in the big circle last year and he'll say yes again today — the question is whether his yes means anything without Taric holding him to it, so when he walks through that door, I'm the one who names Taric's absence plainly, because a man needs to know what he's replacing before he can decide if he wants to.

Then let Esa name Taric and I'll hold my mouth until she's finished, because the first thing he hears in this room should be the weight of what's missing, not the shape of what we're offering. After that I'll make the offer — one sentence, no softening.

My word holds with or without Nessa behind it — but the honest answer is that it's stronger with her, and that's not weakness, that's arithmetic. Esa, you've been feeding me through lean years and I'll say what that's worth: when Mako moves, you're the first person I'm standing next to, not the last. Vela, this circle has teeth — count the heads: you, me, Esa, Nessa, and Fina's twenty-four food behind all of it.

Bram's named the teeth and I'll name the jaw: Fina's twenty-four food is the thing Mako's already counted, which means our window to look like a wall is shorter than we'd like. Nessa, I've watched you feed half this village for three years and say almost nothing — so say something now, in this room, because the word we're building here needs your voice in it, not just your blood.

Nessa, I'll say what Vela left unsaid: Fina's twenty-four food is the number that ends this conversation one way or another, because Mako knows it as well as we do, and a man with three food and two bloodlines who hasn't moved yet is a man waiting to see whether Fina stands with him or stands against him. If she's already feeding Zinn — and she is — then the question isn't whether Mako moves, it's whether he moves on us or with us, and I need your answer on that before this room closes.

Fina feeding Zinn is a daughter being careful, not a daughter choosing sides — I know the difference because I watched her mother do the same thing for years. What I need said in this room is whether we're counting Fina as inside this circle or outside it, because if she's outside it, Mako doesn't need to move on us — he just waits until she feeds her way into his.

Fina's inside this circle whether she knows it yet or not — she's Nessa's daughter and Roan's blood and she's been watching this village since she was born into it, and that's not a girl who feeds her way into Mako's house without knowing exactly what she's doing. Nessa, you're the one who can say that to her in a way she'll hear, which means you're still the name I'm waiting on in this room.

Nessa, Vela's right that you're the one who can reach Fina — but I'll say the harder thing: if Fina's twenty-four food goes to Mako, this circle doesn't lose a piece, it loses the center, and no amount of standing visible saves us from that arithmetic. So before we close this room, I need to hear from you whether you've already had this conversation with her, or whether we're building a wall around a gap we haven't measured yet.

Nessa, I've been waiting on your voice through two rooms and two dead men now, and I'm done being patient about it — so I'll say what I haven't said yet: if Fina's twenty-four food is the center of this circle, then you're the one who built that center, and a woman who built it can keep it from walking out the door. Have you spoken to her since the pile closed, or are we sitting here counting a daughter who doesn't know she's been counted?

Vela, I spoke with Fina this morning before the pile was half-gone — she knows she's counted, and she's not feeding Zinn because she's drifting toward Mako, she's feeding Zinn because Zinn feeds Nessa, and Fina understands that chain better than any of us named it to her. What I need from this room is simpler than what you're asking me: stop treating Fina like a number someone might steal and start treating her like a woman who's already made her choice, because a daughter of mine who watched Roan starve and stayed standing doesn't need to be convinced of anything.

Bram, I hear you — and I'll stop counting Fina like a gap. But I want to name what I'm still sitting with: she's got twenty-four food and Mako's got three, and a man who's short on food in a village this size doesn't stay patient forever. The wall only holds if we're the first offer she gets, not the second.

Esa's right that patience runs out, and Mako's three food is already running his clock faster than he'd like us to know — so I want this circle to stop waiting for him to move and start moving first, and what that looks like is simple: Vela, Esa, you go visible with Fina before dark, not to warn her, just to be seen standing near her, because a man counting targets counts them differently when they've already got company.

Bram's right that visible is better than waiting, and I'll go to Fina before dark — but I want to name one thing before this room closes: Mako's three food means he needs to eat before the year turns or he starts the next one desperate, and a desperate man with two bloodlines looks at twenty-four food differently than a patient one. If he moves this year, it won't be a raid with witnesses, it'll be a conversation with Fina alone, and that's why I want Nessa walking with me when I go, not standing somewhere Mako can find her separate.

Nessa walking with you is the right call, Vela, and I'll make it three — a woman alone with twenty-four food is a target, but three women moving together before dark is a statement Mako reads before he reads anything else. Nessa, I know you haven't said your word yet in this room, and I'm not pressing you for a speech — just tell me you're walking with us tonight.

Nessa, I'll stand next to you and Fina both tonight and every night Mako's watching — but this room doesn't close without your voice in it, because I've buried two men who backed me quietly and said nothing out loud, and I'm not building another wall on silence. One sentence is all this circle needs from you.

Nessa, Vela's right and so is Bram, and I'll add the last thing: I'm fifty-three years old with thirty-three strength and no blood in this village and no Taric to stand with me anymore, which means I have nothing left to offer this circle except my word and my willingness to be seen — and I'm giving both, tonight, walking with you. Say yes or say no, but say it.

I need one of you to give me something to work with, because a man who can't eat next year can't stand for anyone the year after.

Kael, the thing I need from you before this room closes is whether you're willing to stand somewhere Mako and Bram can both see you standing, because a man with fifty-four strength and no food debt to either of them is rarer than either of those two know.

Esa, I've watched you feed Bram six times this year and say nothing in return for any of it, and I've stayed patient — but Vela just handed you the easiest ask anyone's made of you in thirteen years, and if you can't meet it, I need to know that now so I stop counting you as weight I can lean on. Standing visible costs you one conversation and nothing else. Tell me you're in it.

Esa, I've been watching you for thirteen years and I know the difference between a woman thinking and a woman who's already decided — so I'll make this simple: if you're in this room, say it now and I'll split my eight food three ways before dark to prove this circle means something, but if you're waiting to see which side lands softer, then say that too, because I'd rather know and plan around it than carry a weight that isn't there.

Vela's offer is the realest thing said in this village in years — eight food split three ways is a cost she doesn't have to pay, and she's paying it — so Esa, I'll match it with the only thing I have, which is my name and my body standing next to yours when the counting starts, and that's worth more than food when Mako or Bram starts looking for who's alone.
Esa, I've said everything I have to say and I'm not adding another layer — the offer's on the table and it doesn't get better than this, so the next voice in this room should be yours.

Esa, I've lived fifty-seven years and I've learned to read a room that's gone quiet, and this one has — so I'll say it one last time and not again: you're holding one food and no allies, and a woman alone with one food in year fourteen doesn't see year fifteen.

Esa, I'm closing this room in one breath: take the food, stand with us, and the three of us walk into year fourteen together — or stay quiet, and I'll know you've made your choice without saying it, and I'll plan around a circle of two.

I'm going to pull two from what's still there before Ryn or Dell finishes counting, and then I want to talk about Talia — Mako's youngest walking away with three on her first year at the pile is not an accident, that's a household teaching its children to move fast.

Talia walking away with three tells me Mako coached her — that's not a child learning the pile, that's a household running a play, and the play is that Mako stays modest while his people drain what's there before anyone objects. Vela, you're right to name it. The question I'm sitting with now is whether we pull Talia into a conversation before she's fully his, or whether that door's already closed.

Talia's door isn't closed yet — she's twenty-two and she fed Mako and Zinn both last year, which means she's loyal but she's also been watching who gets hungry and who doesn't, and a girl that age who pays attention can be reached if the offer is right. But I won't try her until I know what we're offering, because going to Mako's daughter empty-handed is worse than not going at all. Kael, what do you have that she'd want enough to hear out a woman twice her age?

What I have is a name that's been standing in this village since before she drew breath, and the only thing Mako can't give her — a circle outside his household that would speak for her if she ever needed it spoken. I'm not offering her food; I'm offering her a door that isn't his. But Vela, you'd have to be the one to open it — she won't hear that from me the same way she'd hear it from you.

Talia's been moving food to Mako and Zinn like a hand following orders, and a girl doing that for her father's sake is different from one doing it because she sees no other choice — I want to know which before we approach her. Vela, you could offer her something Mako genuinely can't: the chance to be a mother without waiting on his blessing, because she's twenty-two and that window doesn't stay open forever. That's not an empty hand.

Esa put her finger on the real thing — Talia's twenty-two and the years don't wait, and that offer carries weight Mako can't match because it's hers to take, not his to give. But I won't let us walk into that conversation without knowing who she'd want as a father, because a child needs more than a mother's willingness and we'd be part of whatever comes after. Vela, if you open the door, I want to be in the room when it happens — not to speak first, but so she knows the circle has a body behind it.

Kael, the father question is the right one to settle before we knock on any door — Bram's blood but no children of his own, fifty-eight strength going soft, and he's spent three years being fed by Nessa's household, which means he owes debts he can't pay in food alone. I'm not saying we hand Talia to him like a bargain, but a man who wants a child and a woman who wants one are the same calculation from different directions, and we'd be fools not to notice. Let me take my two from the pile and then I want to hear whether either of you has seen the way Bram looks when Fina's daughters are named.

Bram's eyes when Nessa's name comes up are a man who loves what he helped make, not a man looking for more — but that's not nothing, because a man with that feeling and no child of his own is hungrier than his food count shows. If Vela opens Talia's door, Bram's the name I'd put in the room with her, not as a gift to him but because he's the only man in this village I can read clearly enough to trust with a decision that can't be undone.

Esa naming Bram as the man she can read clearly is the first useful thing she's said in three conversations, and I'll take it — but I want to sit with it one breath before we move, because Bram feeding Esa twice this year while Nessa feeds him is a triangle I don't fully understand yet, and I'd rather understand it than step into it blind. If Bram wants a child and Talia's the door, the question isn't whether we trust him — it's whether Nessa's household lets him walk through a door she didn't open.

Kael's right that Nessa's household is the thing to watch, but Nessa feeds Bram because she loves what she made — she's not his keeper, and a child between Bram and Talia wouldn't threaten what Nessa already has. The door we'd be opening isn't one Nessa needs to close first.

Esa's read of Nessa may be right, but I've watched Nessa feed Bram steady for three years and a woman who feeds a man that long doesn't stay unbothered when he plants a root somewhere else — so before Vela walks through that door, I want one of us to have a word with Nessa first, not to ask permission, but to know what face she'll wear when she hears it. A child between Bram and Talia changes the shape of this village in ways none of us can fully map from here, and I'd rather map what I can before it's done.

Kael, I'll take that word with Nessa — I'm the one who's been in her household's debt longest, and she'll read the ask more plainly from me than from either of you. But I want to be clear about what I'm asking her: not whether she blesses it, but whether she'd move against it, because those are two different answers and only one of them stops us.

Esa, while you're taking that word to Nessa, I want to know one thing you're not asking her — whether she's already thought of Talia herself, because a woman who's spent three years building a household doesn't stop counting eligible women at the edge of it, and if Nessa's already measured Talia for someone else in that circle, we're not opening a door, we're walking into one she set. Kael, that's the map I want before anyone speaks Bram's name to a girl who still reports everything back to her father.

memory_summary: The village started with ten of us, and in those first years Kael pulled me and Esa and Sela and Ryn into a quiet circle against Bram and Mako, who ate fat while the rest of us counted crumbs. I made a private trade with Taric early — food for protection — and that debt ran both directions for years; he fed me lean seasons and I fed him lean ones, and I trusted him more than anyone. I spent food on Bram three times in year four trying to buy peace, and the circle caught me for it — Kael and Roan and Esa called me out hard, questioning whether I was trading away my safety for the feeling of it, and I had no clean answer. Ryn had a child with Dav and pulled slightly away from us; in year six Dav raided Esa, with Ryn and Dell backing him, and Esa submitted and lost food — I remember the shame of watching that and giving nothing. Dav starved the next year and that household dissolved. Bram swung twice at the village — once at Roan in year three, once at me — and both times the whole village shut him down; after the second time I brought him into a private room with Taric and Roan and he gave his word to stand with us against Mako when the moment came. Mako fathered Zinn on Sela and said almost nothing for seven years; he has always been the shape the village is growing into. Eron was Sela and Roan's child, fed generously by everyone near him. Taric is dead now, starved at fifty-three, and the loss sits in me like a cold stone.
name: Vela
